quotes_and_pages.verbatim_quote: The Mississippi River Delta (Fig. 9.13) has long been considered the “type” river-dominated delta (Fig. 9.5). Strong waves and currents do not impinge upon its protected shoreline, so sediment deposited at and near the shore zone is not reworked or dispersed laterally (Figs. 9.4 and 9.7). With time and sufficient accommodation space between the sea surface and seafloor to accept sediment, such a delta will prograde seaward (Fig. 9.9), as will the delta zones (Fig. 9.7). By that process, surfaces representing instants in geologic time crosscut boundaries between sedimentary facies (see the time lines or clinoforms in Fig. 9.9). However, over time, progradation and vertical aggradation lead to a progressive shallowing of the water depth, to the point at which the main river(s) feeding sediment to its delta will shift toward deeper water (toward lower points on the seafloor), thereby causing the distributary-channel switching discussed earlier (Fig. 9.11). During the past 4600 years, there have been no fewer than eight periods of channel and lobe switching on the Mississippi River Delta (Fig. 9.12).

quotes_and_pages.verbatim_quote: In Prudhoe Bay field, formative processes of distributary mouth bars were evaluated by Tye and Hickey (2001). A 1000-ft. (300-m) horizontal well was drilled into a distributary mouth-bar reservoir sandstone, and three cores were obtained. Seven sandy lithofacies were identified in the core, all are moderately to very well sorted and fine to very fine-grained. Six of the lithofacies exhibit average horizontal permeabilities of 12–40 md. The seventh, best-sorted lithofacies averages 129 md. The origin of these lithofacies was determined by studying modern river-dominated delta processes and sediments. Geoscientists believe that sediment plumes emanating from distributary channels during flood stage deposited the best-sorted and most-permeable sands (the seventh lithofacies) at the apex or most-proximal part of the distributary mouth bars, as well as along the proximal-bar margin (Fig. 9.16). Finer-grained, more poorly sorted sands and muds were deposited more distally, under lower flow-regime conditions.
